stem: A 76-year-old woman is referred to the Urology Clinic with incontinence 2–3 times per day where she has an uncontrollable urge to pass urine. She often does not make it to the toilet in time. She has osteoarthritis of both hips and is awaiting bilateral elective hip replacements. Her BMI is 23 kg/m 2. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Detrusor overactivity
This patient is displaying classical urge incontinence, which is driven by detrusor overactivity. Interventions to improve symptoms can include a reduction in caffeine intake and bladder training. Where patients fail to respond to these interventions, treatment with anticholinergic drugs can be considered, although risks and benefits should be viewed against data suggesting they are associated with cognitive impairment in long-term use.

Bladder outflow obstruction
Bladder outflow obstruction is associated with continuous feelings of a full bladder, pain during urination, problems starting urination and uneven flow. The most common cause of bladder outflow obstruction is prostatic hypertrophy.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner after developing a rash on her leg one week after returning from a camping trip. On examination, there is a large erythematous patch on her left lateral thigh expanding from a red papule at the centre. She reports flu-like symptoms and generalised arthralgia. What is the most likely composition of this patient's rash?
explanation:
Erythema migrans
The correct underlying diagnosis in this patient is Lyme disease. Erythema migrans is pathognomonic for this condition and appears in 50–90% of patients within 1–2 weeks of an infected tick bite from an endemic area.

Erythema ab igne
Erythema ab igne describes the reticulated pattern of erythema and hyperpigmentation seen after repeat exposure to heat. This is classically seen after prolonged hot-water-bottle use or sitting close to a fire.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme describes immune-mediated mucocutaneous target lesions which are usually self- limiting. Lesions are typically widespread, unlike the single lesion described in the case here. Approximately 90% of cases of erythema multiforme are driven by infections, including herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, influenza and COVID-19. Lyme disease does not cause erythema multiforme.

stem: A 36-year-old man is referred to the Psychiatric Clinic concerned that he has trouble expressing his emotions. He says that he always feels cold towards others and finds it difficult to have fun doing things that others would find entertaining. He has been in the same job for the past nine years. What is the most accurate description of his personality?
explanation:
Schizoid personality disorder
Patients with a schizoid personality disorder are cold or not interested in others and usually choose to be alone. They find it difficult to express emotions and cannot take pleasure in activities which others enjoy. Sexual relationships with others are difficult and this frequently leads to relationship breakdown.

Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder patients have an absolute fear of being left alone or abandoned. They see themselves as being unstable or weak and this is often reflected in an inability to form long-term relationships.

Histrionic personality disorder
Patients with histrionic personality disorder always seek attention and are overtly dramatic. They are easily led by others and have shallow emotions which change quickly.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with haematuria and proteinuria for the past three months. Her symptoms commenced with frank haematuria 36 hourrs after an upper respiratory tract infection. She takes ramipril for BP control. Her BP is 138/73 mmHg and heart rate is 67 bpm and regular. She has pitting oedema of both ankles. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 123 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count 7.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l (WCC) C-reactive protein 49 mg/l < 10 mg/l (CRP) Platelets (PLT) 203 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 132 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Urine dipstick Blood 1+, protein 2+ Areas of focal glomerulosclerosis, mesangial Renal biopsy hypercellularity What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Immunoglobulin A nephropathy
Immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy most commonly presents with frank haematuria occurring 24–48 hours after the onset of an upper respiratory tract infection. Where there is persistent haematuria and proteinuria, a renal biopsy is indicated to confirm the diagnosis and show evidence of focal glomerulosclerosis, as is seen here. Corticosteroids may be indicated for some patients with IgA nephropathy where there is evidence of active inflammation. In addition to use of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, evolving clinical trials suggest that SGLT-2 inhibitors may also be of benefit.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease
Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease is associated with pulmonary and renal haemorrhage. Renal biopsy shows crescenteric glomerulonephritis.

Lupus nephritis
Lupus nephritis presents in patients who have other features of the disease including a photosensitive rash and small-joint polyarthritis. The timing of the onset of symptoms here is more suggestive of IgA nephropathy. Renal biopsy in patients with lupus shows subendothelial immune deposits.

Membranous glomerulonephritis
Membranous glomerulonephritis is associated with marked proteinuria which may be in the nephrotic range. Light microscopy reveals thickened glomerular capillary loops without hyper-cellularity.

Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is characterised by haematuria which begins 1–3 weeks after a group A streptococcal infection. A diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis is seen rather than the focal glomerulosclerosis on this patient's biopsy.

stem: A 26-year-old woman, who works at a local flour factory, is referred to the Respiratory Clinic for investigation of shortness of breath and wheeze. She feels that they symptoms are worse when she is at work and resolve when she is off work or on holiday. Examination in the clinic after a period on holiday is unremarkable. There is no wheeze on auscultation of the chest. What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
Serial peak flows
Serial peak flow measurements are the most useful initial investigation in suspected occupational asthma. Peak flow is likely to be significantly decreased in the morning and evening during days at work, and recovery will be seen at weekends and during periods of holiday. The most important next step after the diagnosis is confirmed is to examine work practice to ensure that exposure to allergens, in this case flour dust, is minimised.

Chest CT scan
A chest CT scan is most useful in confirming underlying restrictive lung disease by demonstrating evidence of pulmonary fibrosis. The symptoms here are much more suggestive of occupational asthma, for which serial peak flow measurements are the most useful next investigation.

stem: A 20-year-old man is admitted on the Surgical Ward with small-bowel obstruction. He admits to weight loss and night sweats over the past three months. Laparotomy is performed, and biopsy of a suspicious lesion has confirmed Burkitt's lymphoma. Which translocation is most likely to be present in this patient?
explanation:
t(8;14)(q24;q32)
This translocation between chromosomes 8 and 14 is characteristic of Burkitt's lymphoma. It produces a fusion protein which leads to lymphocyte proliferation. Sporadic Burkitt's lymphoma as here is seen in developed nations, can occur in adults and is associated with Epstein–Barr virus. Abdominal and pelvic organs are commonly involved. Rituximab is usually given with combination chemotherapy, as in initial treatment, the risk of tumour-lysis syndrome is very high.

t(9;22)(q34;q11)
This translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22 is known as the Philadelphia chromosome. It is found most commonly in chronic myelogenous leukaemia and acute lymphoblastic leukaemia. It drives increased cell division and reduced apoptosis.

stem: A 61-year-old man, who has type II diabetes and hypertension, is brought to the Emergency Department after collapsing. He has persistent vomiting and is unable to mobilise. He has become progressively drowsy over the past hour and has evidence of nystagmus and a bulbar palsy. He has peripheral vascular disease and has had a previous left femoral endarterectomy. There is global weakness. A magnetic resonance angiogram is suggestive of basilar artery occlusion. A thrombectomy is planned. Which artery should be cannulated?
explanation:
Brachial
This patient has a posterior circulation stroke because of occlusion of the basilar artery. In this case removal of the thrombus is crucial to improving recovery because of the poor performance of thrombolysis as an alternative. Cannulation of the brachial artery avoids the tortuosity afforded by femoral cannulation, and the basilar artery can be accessed via the vertebral arteries. In this case, it is likely to prove difficult to cannulate the femoral artery given the history of peripheral vascular disease and previous surgery. The clot can then be aspirated or removed.

Axillary
The axillary artery is not preferred for cannulation because pressure cannot be easily applied to the site of catheter entry. The brachial artery is the usual preferred approach.

stem: A 74-year-old man who has Lewy body dementia, is brought to the Emergency Department with nausea, vomiting and abdominal distention. His abdomen is firm with moderate distension. He is suspected to have small-bowel obstruction. What is the most appropriate antiemetic to manage his symptoms?
explanation:
Ondansetron
Ondansetron is a centrally acting 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT3)-receptor-antagonist antiemetic. It therefore does not have a negative impact on symptoms of pain associated with bowel obstruction or impact on movement disorder linked to Lewy Body dementia. It can be dosed up to 8 mg every 8–12hrs. It can lead to QT prolongation in some patients.

Domperidone
Although domperidone is associated with fewer extrapyramidal side-effects than metoclopramide and prochlorperazine it still has some D2-antagonist properties; for this reason, ondansetron, a 5-HT3 antagonist, is preferred.

stem: A 72-year-old woman who has ischaemic heart disease, type II diabetes, hypertension and lumbar spine radiculopathy is referred to the Ambulatory Care Clinic with pitting oedema of both lower limbs, She is otherwise stable and able to manage her own activities of daily living. Her BP is 145/85 mmHg and her heart rate is 65 bpm and regular. There are no crackles on auscultation of the chest. There is pitting oedema to the mid-shins bilaterally. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of her peripheral oedema?
explanation:
Pregabalin
Pregabalin is used in combination with analgesics to manage nerve-root pain. It is an under-recognised cause of peripheral oedema, thought to be caused by binding to the alpha-2 gamma subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels. More commonly recognised causes of lower limb pitting oedema include dihydropyridine-calcium antagonists such as amlodipine and alpha-blockers such as doxazosin.

Codeine
Codeine is an opiate analgesic not recognised as a cause of peripheral oedema. In this case, pregabalin is most likely responsible for the patient's symptoms. Ideally, the patient's use of codeine should be rationalised, as it is likely to be ineffective in controlling her nerve-root pain and is sedating, particularly in the elderly.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to the Obstetric Clinic for a routine check-up. She is 30 weeks' pregnant and has been feeling tired recently. Levels of which maternal pituitary hormone are recognised to fall in pregnancy?
explanation:
Growth hormone
Pituitary growth hormone levels rise initially in pregnancy but around week 15–17 a progressive fall begins. This is because placental growth hormone increases significantly, driving hepatic production of insulin-like growth-factor 1 (IGF1). The IGF1 then participates in a negative feedback loop with the pituitary to turn off pituitary growth hormone production.

Adrenocorticotrophic hormone
Adrenocorticotrophic hormone levels rise progressively during pregnancy. Although there is a 2–3-fold overall increase in cortisol levels during pregnancy, women do not generally display signs of hypercortisolism during pregnancy.

Oxytocin
Oxytocin levels rise from the first to the third trimester of pregnancy and then fall during the postpartum period. Oxytocin antagonists may have a role to play in halting premature labour.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is reviewed in the Rheumatology Clinic for pain in her right knee. Flexion is limited and she tells you she has pain on weight bearing which is limiting her exercise. Her BMI is 31 kg/m 2. An X-ray reveals joint-space narrowing and osteophyte formation consistent with right-knee osteoarthritis. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Swimming
Exercise which can lead to strengthening of muscles around the knee and drive energy loss is recommended as initial management of osteoarthritis. Patients should be warned that when they initiate exercise, pain may increase. Over time, exercise such as swimming leads to a reduction in knee pain and increased exercise tolerance.

Acupuncture
Acupuncture is not recommended for the treatment of knee osteoarthritis. Other interventions such as manipulation, ultrasound or electrotherapy are also not recommended.

Knee brace
Knee braces are not recommended in the treatment of osteoarthritis because they may actually weaken muscles surrounding the knee and precipitate further pain and instability. Exercise is the recommended initial intervention.

stem: A 37-year-old man who is known to have HIV is referred to the Dermatology Clinic with a number of skin lesions that have increased over the past six months. He has a mix of nodular and macular erythematous purple lesions, and says they have both grown in size and number. They are also affecting his mucous membranes. What is the most likely cause of his skin lesions?
explanation:
Human herpes virus 8
Human herpes virus 8 is the cause of this patient's skin lesions which are likely to be Kaposi's sarcomas. In addition to skin and mucous membranes, internal organs may also be affected by Kaposi's skin lesions, which can bleed. Starting antiretroviral therapy for underlying HIV leads to a reduction in Kaposi's lesions in around 40% of patients. Systemic therapy with interferon-alpha may also be of value.

Human herpes virus 2
Human herpes virus 2 is the cause of oral herpes, characterised by cold sores. It may also cause genital herpes which is characterised by extremely painful small vesicular lesions which can lead to urinary retention in women.

Human herpes virus 4
Human herpes virus 4 is the alternative name for Epstein–Barr virus which causes symptoms of pharyngitis and may result in a viral hepatitis. It is also a risk factor for the development of Hodgkin's lymphoma.

stem: A 20-year-old man is referred to the Immunology Clinic because of frequent lower respiratory tract infections and intermittent diarrhoea. His chest his clear on auscultation. His BMI is 19 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 137 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.4 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Immunoglobulin G (IgG) 4.0 g/l 6.0–16.0 g/l Immunoglobulin A (IgA) 0.6 g/l 0.8–2.8 g/l Immunoglobulin M (IgM) 1.2 g/l 0.5–1.9 g/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Common variable immunodeficiency
Common variable immunodeficiency leads to a modest reduction in both IgG and IgA and increased risk of both respiratory and GI infections. It is thought to be due to a partial defect in B-cell maturation. Risk of bronchiectasis is increased, as is the risk of B-cell lymphoma and gastric cancer. Immunoglobulin replacement therapy can delay the development of bronchiectasis and improve quality of life. A range of autoimmune diseases is also seen more frequently in patients with the disease.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is referred to the Renal Clinic with hypertension and chronic kidney disease. She suffered from multiple UTIs as a child. Her BP is 155/95 mmHg and heart rate is 78 bpm and regular. Her BMI is 23 kg/m 2. There are no abdominal masses. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 98 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.1 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 181 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 140 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 193 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l What is the most likely cause of her renal impairment?
explanation:
Vesicoureteral reflux
Given this patient's history of multiple UTIs as a child, no abnormal findings on abdominal examination and anaemia with elevated creatinine, chronic vesicoureteric reflux leading to renal impairment seems the most likely diagnosis. Renal scarring can be avoided by prompt treatment with antibiotics in children when a UTI is identified, and surgical correction when significant reflux of urine is confirmed.

stem: A 34-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with chronic tiredness. A blood test reveals an immunoglobulin M (IgM) paraprotein band. A diagnosis of Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia (WM) is suspected. Which of the following is the most prominent presenting feature of WM?
explanation:
Headache and blurred vision
Hyperviscosity is the cardinal feature of WM and leads to symptoms in around 30% of patients with the condition. Symptoms include headaches, blurred vision and dizziness, and they are often what causes patients to seek medical attention. Symptoms of hyperviscosity indicate a need for urgent intervention with a rituximab- based regimen being the treatment of choice. Median survival of WM is around five years.

Lymphadenopathy
Lymphadenopathy is found in a considerable number of patients with WM, but is marginally less common than symptoms of hyperviscosity at presentation, found in around 25% of patients.

Lytic bone lesions
Lytic bone lesions are a feature of myeloma and are much less commonly seen in patients with WM. One series of 271 patients with WM identified no patients with lytic lesions at presentation.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is reviewed in the renal clinic with symptoms of acidosis, hyponatraemia and hypokalaemia. She has recently completed chemotherapy for breast cancer. What is the likely site of her renal injury?
explanation:
Proximal tubule
Around 70% of solutes including sodium, potassium, bicarbonate and glucose are reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. A number of drugs can lead to proximal tubular dysfunction and lead to the clinical picture seen here. Ifosamide and oxaplatin are examples of chemotherapy agents known to result in proximal renal tubular acidosis. The sodium–glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2) channel, the site of action of SGLT-2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin, lies in the proximal tubule.

Collecting duct
The main role of the collecting duct is in reabsorption of water. This occurs via aquaporin-2 channels, the expression of which is partially regulated by antidiuretic hormone.

Distal tubule
Most solutes are already reabsorbed by the time that filtrate reaches the distal tubule. stem: A 67-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic with features of Parkinson's disease which have responded poorly to intervention with levodopa therapy. He has a broad-based gait with increased limb rigidity and a mild jerky tremor, more marked on the left than the right. There are extensor plantar responses. and a 30 mmHg fall in systolic BP moving from lying to standing. He has mild cognitive impairment. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multi-system atrophy
Multi-system atrophy (MSA) is a neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a combination of Parkinsonian features, cerebellar signs, autonomic dysfunction and pyramidal involvement. This patient exhibits a poor response to levodopa, significant postural hypotension and extensor plantar responses, all of which point away from idiopathic Parkinson’s disease and towards an atypical Parkinsonian syndrome. Autonomic dysfunction, such as a ≥30 mmHg systolic drop on standing, is particularly suggestive of MSA, especially when it occurs early in the disease course. The presence of a broad-based gait and cognitive changes can occur in MSA, although dementia is typically less prominent than in conditions like dementia with Lewy bodies.

Multi-infarct dementia

stem: A 32-year-old woman who has primary pulmonary hypertension comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review. She is currently treated with sildenafil and ambrisentan but feels her exercise tolerance has worsened over the past few months and she has swelling of both ankles. A decision is made to start her on iloprost. What is the mode of action of iloprost?
explanation:
Prostacyclin analogue
Iloprost is a prostacyclin analogue that inhibits platelet aggregation, platelet adhesion and leads to dilation of arterioles and venuoles. It also has anti-inflammatory effects and promotes fibrinolysis. Use in patients with primary pulmonary hypertension has been shown to improve outcomes and has a significant impact on exercise tolerance. Iloprost is given as an infusion; oral prostacyclin-receptor agonists are no longer available as an alternative.

Calcium-channel antagonist
Calcium-channel antagonists such as amlodipine are used early in the treatment of primary pulmonary hypertension. A small percentage of patients are responsive to these agents and could potentially benefit before moving on to conventional therapies such as endothelin-receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitors and iloprost.

stem: A 36-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic with Raynaud’s phenomenon, which has responded poorly to calcium channel blockers. She reports progressive difficulty swallowing and tightening of the skin over her hands and face. She also experiences increasing shortness of breath on exertion. On examination, there are multiple telangiectasias on her face and lips, and she has marked perioral skin tightening with reduced mouth opening. Her fingers show sclerodactyly with firm subcutaneous nodules over the fingertips. Fine inspiratory crackles are heard at the lung bases. Which autoantibody is most strongly associated with this patient’s likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anti-topoisomerase-1
The features in this case — including diffuse skin thickening, calcinosis, oesophageal dysmotility, Raynaud’s phenomenon, telangiectasia, and interstitial lung disease — are most consistent with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Anti-topoisomerase-1 (also known as Scl-70) antibodies are strongly associated with this subtype and are predictive of pulmonary fibrosis and a more severe disease course.

Anti-centromere
Anti-centromere antibodies are typically seen in patients with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (formerly CREST syndrome), which is associated with a lower risk of interstitial lung disease but a higher risk of pulmonary hypertension. The presence of widespread skin involvement and pulmonary fibrosis in this case makes this antibody less likely.

stem: A trial testing the cholesterol-lowering effect of red-yeast rice (a Chinese food supplement) in lowering low- density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol is designed. There are 50 patients per arm (active and placebo), and six months of therapy is planned. What is the most appropriate statistical test to analyse the results?
explanation:
Student's t-test
A t-test is used to compare the means of two groups of data that are normally distributed. In this case, LDL cholesterol is normally distributed, and the t-test allows comparison between the active group (red-yeast rice) and the placebo group. In this type of trial, a P value < 0.05 would be considered significant with respect to the difference in cholesterol between groups.

Chi-squared test
The Chi-squared test is used to compare binary data between two or more groups of data. In this case, cholesterol is a continuous variable, so it is the t-test that is most appropriate to determine whether there is a significant difference between the two groups.

Kruskal–Wallis test
The Kruskal–Wallis test is used to determine whether different samples originate from the same distribution. It is a non-parametric test. Here, the t-test is most appropriate to compare the means of the two groups treated.

stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a generalised rash with tense bullae, which is particularly affecting skin over flexural surfaces. The rash appears to heal without scarring, and she tells you that she has suffered from it for some months. She has had minor blistering affecting her palate, although these lesions like others have healed quickly. She was started on naproxen therapy for osteoarthritis of her hip some 6 months earlier. Routine blood testing reveals a raised ESR. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bullous pemphigoid
The trunk, extremity flexures, and axillary and inguinal folds are common sites for cutaneous involvement. Mucosal lesions are present in 10 to 30 percent of patients ( in pemphigus vulgaris almost all patient develop mucosal involvement and buccal mucosa and palatine mucosa is most common location where lesions can be severe) . The oral mucosa is the most frequent location of mucosal involvement. Less frequently, bullous pemphigoid involves other mucosal sites, such as the larynx, genitals, and anus. Nail changes may also develop. Pemphigoid may be related in onset to the introduction of medications including furosemide, NSAIDs, captopril and penicillamine.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis primarily affects extensor surfaces such as the elbows, knees, and buttocks with intensely itchy vesicular eruptions. stem: A 21-year-old man, originally from Syria, presents to his General Practitioner with a small ulcer on his forehead. It apparently started as a small spot (which he thought was an insect bite) a couple of months ago and has subsequently gradually ulcerated. On examination, there is a single, ulcerated lesion 2 cm in diameter on his left temple, with raised edges and a fibrous crust. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Leishmaniasis
Leishmaniasis is a heterogeneous group of diseases all caused by different species of the protozoa Leishmania. All species are transmitted via a sandfly bite. There are two distinct clinical forms caused by different species – cutaneous (or mucocutaneous) and visceral. The two forms present very differently, which needs to be considered when you see leishmaniasis as a possible answer to an exam question. Cutaneous disease presents with a nodule 1–2 months after the infected sandfly bite, which gradually ulcerates, often with a thick fibrous crust over the surface. Cutaneous disease is particularly prevalent in South America and in Asian countries around the Old Silk Road – including Syria or other areas in the Middle East that this patient may have travelled through.

Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinomas are slow-growing skin malignancies that can eventually ulcerate and could present in this sort of manner. stem: A 31-year-old man was found to have hepatitis C infection. He was originally from Egypt and denied any blood transfusions or previous injecting-drug use. His mother died of jaundice 20 years ago. His only past medical history was as a young child in Egypt, where he remembered having blood in his urine and being treated for a ‘bladder infection’. How is this patient most likely to have contracted hepatitis C?
explanation:
Vertical transmission
Whilst vertical transmission of hepatitis C is relatively rare, it is the most likely cause of transmission amongst the options given here – the information given that his mother died from jaundice makes it likely that she had hepatitis C too.

Contact with the local population
Hepatitis C is typically spread through blood-to-blood contact, meaning that contact with the local population is not a possible cause of transmission.

Contaminated drinking water
While hepatitis A and E are transmitted through the faeco-oral route, hepatitis C is not, and contaminated drinking water is therefore not the explanation here.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner, as she has failed to gain control of her rheumatoid arthritis symptoms, despite use of two different tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha antagonists. The addition of a T-cell co-stimulation modulator is considered, to control her symptoms. Which receptor on T lymphocytes is involved in co-stimulation?
explanation:
CD28
The CD28 receptor on T lymphocytes is the receptor for the CD80 and CD86 proteins. It is one of the co- stimulatory receptors which drives T-cell activation, alongside cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen 4. Blockade of co-stimulatory receptors is a target for treatments against autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. Agonists of co-stimulatory receptors act as anti-cancer agents.

CD3
CD3 receptors are found on T lymphocytes. Monoclonal antibodies which bind to T lymphocytes lead to immune tolerance by promoting inactivity in T-effector cells and upregulation of T-regulatory cells.

CD14
CD14 is produced by human macrophages. It helps detect and clear bacterial infection by binding to lipopolysaccharide which then promotes immune-mediated clearance.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is reviewed in the Pharmacology Clinic for management of her hypertension. Her current BP is 180/100 mmHg. What is the most important cause of her raised pulse pressure?
explanation:
Aortic stiffness
Progressive stiffness and loss of large-vessel elasticity – including in the aorta – leads to a widening of pulse pressure in the elderly. This leads to a reduced capacity for the large arteries to absorb the wave of blood which flows out of the left ventricle with each heart beat. Other causes of a wide pulse pressure include aortic regurgitation and high-output heart failure seen in hyperthyroidism.

Left ventricular hypertrophy
Left ventricular hypertrophy leads to an increase in systolic BP but is not the main contributor to increased pulse pressure. It is arterial stiffness leading to a lack of capacitance which is the main contributor to wide pulse pressure.

Pulmonary hypertension
Pulmonary hypertension contributes to the requirement for the right ventricle to increase output. Eventually the right ventricle cannot keep up with required output, leading to peripheral oedema and an elevated jugular venous pressure as signs of right heart failure.

stem: A 32-year-old South Asian woman is referred to the Antenatal Clinic for management of her first pregnancy. She complains of tiredness. On examination, she looks pale and there is no evidence of organomegaly. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 98 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets 154 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 67 fl 79–100 fl HbA2 6% 1.5–3.1% HbF 4% < 2% Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Beta thalassaemia trait
This patient has beta thalassaemia trait. Patients commonly present with microcytic anaemia which can be mistaken for iron deficiency. The increased HbA2 level suggests beta thalassaemia trait. stem: A 72-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with her son. He says that over the last six months she has been found lost in the neighbourhood she has recently moved to. She has missed sending birthday cards to several relatives over the last two years, and her sleep is broken. She is unable to recall what she ate for breakfast but says she has no memory difficulties. She seems apathetic and her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 24/30 with points lost for orientation and recall. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most appropriate initial therapy?
explanation:
Donepezil
Given the deficits in episodic memory and executive dysfunction, the likely diagnosis is Alzheimer's disease. Acetylcholinesterase-inhibitor treatment (donepezil, galantamine or rivastigmine) should be considered in patients with mild or moderate disease, although this should ideally be initiated by a specialist.

Lorazepam
Lorazepam and other benzodiazepines may be used for short-term control of acute agitation or disturbed sleep patterns. They do not alter the underlying pathophysiological processes in dementia, which is why donepezil (or memantine) would be a better option.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is reviewed in the Oncology Clinic following a left breast lumpectomy for cancer. She is to be treated with trastuzumab as part of her therapy. What is the mode of action of trastuzumab?
explanation:
HER2 inhibitor
Trastuzumab is an immunoglobulin G (IgG) monoclonal antibody directed against HER2. HER2 is over- expressed in around 20–30% of breast cancers. By blocking, the receptor trastuzumab leads to a reduction in the proliferative stimulus. In clinical trials, progression-free survival was doubled for trastuzumab plus anastrozole versus anastrozole alone. Cardiomyopathy is a significant concern with trastuzumab therapy, and regular echocardiograms are mandated during therapy.

BRAF inhibitor
BRAF inhibitors are used in the treatment of malignant melanoma where the melanoma cells are identified to carry the BRAF mutation. BRAF is a serine/threonine protein kinase which plays a key role in proliferation of melanoma cells.

stem: A 52-year-old man, who has alcoholic cirrhosis, presents to his General Practitioner with sleepiness and ongoing mild confusion consistent with hepatic encephalopathy. He has undergone a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure some three months earlier. What is the most likely cause of his confusion?
explanation:
Hyperammonaemia
TIPS is associated with an increased load of ammonia passing from the portal to the systemic circulation because of stent placement, with levels of ammonia greater than 150 µmol/l potentially leading to severe symptoms of encephalopathy. Reduction of dietary protein and measures to reduce intestinal bacterial load such as rifaximin and lactulose can lead to a reduction in the incidence of encephalopathy.

Hypokalaemia
Hypokalaemia is seen in some patients with alcoholism but is not responsible for this patient's symptoms post- TIPS. It is most commonly seen in response to diuresis related to ingestion of large volumes of alcohol. Most likely, it is accumulation of ammonia in the brain because of placement of the shunt that has led to this patient's confusion.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents with anaemia and is found to have B 12 deficiency. Which of the following is B 12 the most important factor in?
explanation:
Methionine synthesis
Vitamin B 12 is an enzyme cofactor which plays a key role in the activity of methionine synthase which drives the transfer of a methyl group from 5-methyl tetrahydrofolate to homocysteine, generating tetrahydrofolate and methionine. Without B 12 as a cofactor, a rise in homocysteine levels is seen. It also acts as a cofactor in the action of L-methylmalonyl-coenzyme A mutase, an enzyme essential for the breakdown of certain amino acids.

Glycogen synthesis
Glycogen synthase is the key enzyme involved in glycogen synthesis. Its activity is upregulated by insulin; glycogenolysis occurs in response to glucagon. B 12 is involved in protein synthesis and protein catabolism.

Homocysteine synthesis
B 12 is a cofactor in the synthesis of methionine from homocysteine. Absence of B 12 therefore leads to an increase in homocysteine levels because of decreased metabolism of the amino acid. B 12 is also a cofactor in amino-acid catabolism.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is admitted to the Acute Medical Ward with ascending weakness which has steadily progressed over the last four days. She is now unable to get up out of a chair. She suffered from a diarrhoeal illness some three weeks earlier. On examination, there is 3/5 flaccid weakness affecting both lower limbs with diminished reflexes. There is no sensory deficit. Forced vital capacity (FVC) is a good indicator of respiratory muscle function and begins to fall before the risk of respiratory failure is significantly increased in patients with Guillain–Barré syndrome.
