stem: A 45-year-old woman, who has lived for many years in Australia, presents to her General Practitioner with an erythematous scaly lesion on her left shin. Biopsy has demonstrated epithelial dysplasia with no signs of malignancy. What is the most appropriate intervention for this lesion?
explanation:
Topical 5-fluorouracil cream
This patient has a history of excess sun exposure having spent many years in Australia. The biopsy is suggestive of an actinic (solar keratosis), which may eventually develop into a squamous cell carcinoma. 0.5% fluorouracil therapy can be used for 6–12 weeks, applied once a day. Salicylic acid, imiquimod and diclofenac topical therapies are potential alternatives. In this case, surgery is best avoided on the shin because of relatively thin tissue between the surface and the tibia.

Curetage
Curetage, like surgery, is not preferred for actinic keratoses occuring on the shin, where there is a relatively thin layer of tissue between the skin and the tibia. Topical therapy such as 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) cream is preferred here.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department (ED) requesting an abdominal CT scan, as she is convinced she has colon cancer. Her uncle died from the condition aged 72. She has attended the ED six times previously and has had both an abdominal CT scan and a colonoscopy. An examination is unremarkable and repeat bloods are normal. What is the most appropriate next intervention?
explanation:
Cognitive behavioural therapy
This patient has illness anxiety disorder and will go on seeking investigations until they are offered cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) as an intervention. They are preoccupied with a possible cancer diagnosis and are continuing to seek further investigations in spite of regular reassurance from their doctors. Where CBT alone is not effective, the addition of a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor such as sertraline can be considered.

Diazepam
Diazepam is only appropriate as a short-term treatment for anxiety. This patient shows marked symptoms of illness anxiety disorder for which CBT is the most appropriate next step.

Repeat abdominal CT scan
Further investigations are not indicated given the normal findings so far. Indeed, requesting another CT is only likely to reinforce behaviour to seek further investigations. Referral for CBT is the most appropriate next step.

stem: A 63-year-old man who has type II diabetes is referred to the Endocrine Clinic for review. He is currently taking linagliptin to control his blood sugar. What is the mode of action of linagliptin?
explanation:
Dipeptidyl peptidase IV inhibitor
Dipeptidyl peptidase IV (DPPIV) inhibitors are oral agents, and linagliptin is one of the class. Other members include agents such as sitagliptin and saxagliptin. By inhibiting DPPIV, they lead to an increase in endogenous levels of glucagon-likepeptide1, glucagon and gastric inhibitory polypeptide, the incretin hormones, and this brings about a modest positive impact on glucose control and a weight loss of maximum 2–3%.

Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
Acarbose is an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor. It blocks breakdown of complex carbohydrates in the gut, reducing glucose absorption from the carbohydrate component of a meal. This improves glucose control with a modest positive impact on weight.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 agonist
Glucagon-like peptide-1 agonists are developed both for weight loss and for control of blood sugar in type II diabetes. They increase insulin release in response to a food challenge and slow gastric emptying. The class may also have central effects in reducing appetite.

stem: A 24-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department with a fever, severe shortness of breath and palpitations over the past three days. He has been suffering from a mild upper respiratory tract infection and diarrhoea for a few days before he became unwell. His BP is 90/50 mmHg and his heart rate is 105 bpm and regular. He has crackles to the mid zones bilaterally on auscultation and pitting oedema of both ankles. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 141 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 55 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 182 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 133 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 131 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Troponin T 729 ng/l < 14 ng/l ECG Widespread T-wave inversion What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Myocarditis
This patient has symptoms consistent with adenovirus infection, following which biventricular failure has developed. This is accompanied by widespread T-wave changes on the ECG and a marked elevation in serum troponin. Taking all of these factors together, the most likely diagnosis is viral myocarditis. Management is similar to that for any other cause of heart failure, with use of diuretics and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors. In this case with hypotension, a ventricular-assist device may also be required. Other viral causes of myocarditis can include parvovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, hepatitis A and C, enteroviruses and influenza. Prognosis is dependent upon aetiology and left ventricular function; patients with markedly reduced ejection fraction may require a transplant.

Brugada syndrome
Brugada syndrome is associated with sudden death; it is not related to post-viral myocarditis. A characteristic ECG pattern is seen in Brugada syndrome with a right bundle branch block morphology.

Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is associated with episodes of collapse due to ventricular arrhythmia and left ventricular outflow-tract obstruction. It does not fit with the clinical picture here of hypotensive heart failure secondary to viral myocarditis.

Myocardial ischaemia
Given this patient is young and has no risk factors for myocardial ischaemia, it is an unlikely cause of his cardiac failure. The symptoms of a viral illness, heart failure and elevation in troponin fit best with a diagnosis of viral myocarditis.

Pericarditis
Pericarditis is associated with widespread T-wave changes, and it follows infections such as adenovirus, suggested by this patient's symptoms. The severity of cardiac failure, and ECG changes, seen here, however, is more consistent with myocarditis.

stem: A 45-year-old man, who is treated with long-term peritoneal dialysis while awaiting a kidney transplant, presents to the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and distension, and incomplete drainage of his overnight bag. The fluid that has drained is cloudy and pus coloured. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Coagulase-negative staphylococci, including S. epidermidis, are responsible for around 60% of cases of dialysis-related peritonitis. This is because the commonest cause of infection is difficulty in maintaining aseptic technique when changing bags, leading to contamination from skin. Causative organisms are usually methicillin resistant, making vancomycin the intervention of choice.

Corynebacterium acnes
Corynebacteria are the cause of around 1 in 20 to 1 in 25 of cases of dialysis-related peritonitis. Coagulase- negative staphylococci are much more likely to be the cause of this patient's symptoms, and vancomycin is the intervention of choice,

stem: A 35-year-old man with uncontrolled hypertension is referred to the Pharmacology Clinic for management of his BP. His General Practitioner referred him for an ultrasound and a left adrenal adenoma was noted. Hyperaldosteronism is suspected. What is the most likely picture on venous blood gas testing?
explanation:
Hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis
In a patient with hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism due to an adrenal adenoma, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis would be expected. This is because aldosterone stimulates sodium and chloride reabsorption and the loss of both hydrogen and potassium ions into the urine. Hypokalaemia often persists, even in patients treated with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers. Measurement of renin and aldosterone levels is useful in confirming the diagnosis.

Hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis
Hyperkalaemic metabolic acidosis is associated with renal tubular acidosis type 4 (which occurs due to deficient aldosterone action). It is also seen in patients with hypocortisolism.

Hyperkalaemic metabolic alkalosis
Hyperkalaemia is not normally associated with metabolic alkalosis. In this situation with hyperaldosteronism, both hydrogen and potassium ions are lost into the urine, leading to a hypokalaemic, alkalotic blood picture.

stem: A 21-year-old man is reviewed in the Orthopaedic Clinic a few weeks after a motorcycle accident. He complains of some weakness in his fingers on the left hand and loss of sensation over his upper chest and the front of his arm. There is weakness of finger abduction affecting the left hand. Which nerve root is most likely to have been injured in this case?
explanation:
T1
The T1 nerve root supplies the muscles of finger abduction and sensation over the front of the arm and part of the upper chest. Injury to T1 therefore fits well with this patient's symptoms. Muscles innervated by the T1 nerve root include flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor policis longus, flexor digitorum profundus, the lumbricals and the interossei. MRI may be useful in demonstrating the injured nerve root.

C5
C5 nerve-root supply is primarily responsible for shoulder abduction. C5 is responsible for some sensation over the front of the chest and the anterior upper arm.

C6
Weakness of elbow flexion and wrist extension is strongly linked to C6 nerve-root injury. Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis are particularly affected. Sensation is lost over the thumb and index finger after C6 nerve- root injury.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is referred to the Oncology Clinic following surgery for breast cancer. Treatment with trastuzumab and doxorubicin is planned. She is aware that use of trastuzumab is associated with increased risk of heart failure. What is most associated with increased risk of heart failure with trastuzumab use?
options: Family history of ischaemic heart disease
explanation:
Co-prescription with doxorubicin
Antagonism of the HER2 receptor by agents such as trastuzumab increases the risk of dilative cardiomyopathy. This has led to a contraindication for use of trastuzumab in patients with an ejection fraction below 55%. Co- prescription of taxanes significantly increases the risk of heart failure occuring during and immediately after trastuzumab therapy. Doxorubicin is thought to downregulate expression of myocardial contractile proteins.

Family history of ischaemic heart disease
The mechanism by which trastuzumab leads to heart failure is not related to myocardial ischaemia. Agonism of the HER2 receptor is protective against dilative cardiomyopathy, and antagonism therefore increases the risk of this occurring.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department stating that he has been sent by God to heal the patients in the hospital. He says he has been communicating with God for the last nine months, and he is now ready to carry out his work. He appears calm, but his speech is tangential, erratic and difficult to follow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Schizophrenia
This patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for a diagnosis of schizophrenia, which requires at least two of: delusions; hallucinations; disorganised speech; disorganised or catatonic behaviour and negative symptoms. Continuous signs of the disturbance must be present for at least six months, during which time the patient must experience at least one month of active symptoms with functional deterioration occurring over a considerable amount of time.

Bipolar affective disorder
Bipolar affective disorder is characterised by predominant disturbances in affect or mood. Psychotic symptoms may be present but are congruent with mania or depression. This patient is clearly exhibiting delusions in addition to auditory hallucinations. There is no mention of mood disorder in the history and there are no comments on disturbed affect.

stem: A 47-year-old man who has idiopathic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia is brought to the Emergency Department following an episode. This is his third episode in the last six weeks. He is currently taking 200 mg of amiodarone per day as a maintenance dose and electrophysiological mapping has suggested the interventricular septum is the source of the arrhythmia. His QT interval is 455 milliseconds (< 450 milliseconds being the normal value). What is the most appropriate way to manage his ventricular tachycardia?
explanation:
Radiofrequency ablation
This patient has idiopathic non-sustained ventricular tachycardia with an apparent septal focus. There is no evidence of structural heart disease, and symptoms are not controlled on amiodarone maintenance. Where the focus of the arrhythmia has been identified, radiofrequency ablation will be the best option. It can control the patient's symptoms and potentially allow amiodarone, which has significant long-term toxicities, to be discontinued.

Implantable cardioverter defibrillator
An implantable cardioverter defibrillator is the intervention of choice to treat non-sustained ventricular tachycardia in patients with end-stage heart failure, cardiomyopathy, Brugada syndrome and high-risk long-QT syndrome. In this case, where a focus of arrhythmia has been identified, radiofrequency ablation is the preferred intervention.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with fever, headache, diarrhoea and neck stiffness. He has recently returned from competing in an open-water swimming event in Hawaii. He soon deteriorates and develops haemoptysis and renal failure. A differential diagnosis including leptospirosis is considered. What is the gold-standard test for confirming a diagnosis of leptospirosis?
explanation:
Microscopic agglutination test
This is the gold standard for diagnosis of leptospirosis and requires the analysis of paired acute and convalescent plasma samples taken two weeks apart. Here, live antigens of leptospires react with patient serum, following which they are examined for agglutination. A fourfold increase between acute and convalescent samples is diagnostic. Given the prolonged wait for a diagnostic result, treatment is normally commenced empirically under the guidance of an Infectious Diseases Team.

Blood culture
While leptospires can be isolated from blood, culture is slow and insensitive. While blood cultures may grow leptospires, they are primarily taken to investigate for other potential bacteraemia.

Chest X-ray
This may demonstrate pulmonary involvement of leptospirosis but will not confirm the diagnosis. Ground-glass opacities may be seen due to pulmonary haemorrhage.

stem: A 45-year-old man who consumes excess alcohol presents to the Emergency Department with worsening abdominal swelling and decreased urine output. His BP is 100/70 mmHg and rate is 75 bpm and regular. He has marked abdominal ascites. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 95 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 6.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 55 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 134 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 61 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l What is the most likely cause of this patient's creatinine level?
explanation:
Decreased muscle mass
Decreased skeletal muscle mass is a common feature of cirrhosis, especially when it is associated with excess alcohol consumption. The level of serum creatinine is determined by muscle mass and dynamic turnover of skeletal muscle cells and renal function. The level is therefore inappropriately normal, instead of high; here, because of sarcopenia.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a 200 ml haemoptysis. He admits to coughing up smaller amounts of blood over the past few days and feeling increasingly unwell with lethargy and a fever. He had a viral respiratory illness two weeks earlier and smokes 30 cigarettes per day. His BP is 149/93 mmHg and heart rate is 98 and regular. There are inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 103 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 10.8 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 13 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 397 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 144 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 5.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 297 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Urine analysis Blood 3+, protein 1+ Renal biopsy Necrotising glomerlonephritis with cellular crescents Chest X-ray Patchy shadowing throughout both lung fields What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease
The clinical picture seen here with pulmonary and renal haemorrhage coupled with deteriorating renal function against a background of heavy smoking and a near-normal CRP is consistent with anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease due to antibodies against the GBM. High-dose corticosteroids are the usual initial intervention, with plasma exchange to remove anti-GBM antibodies being the mainstay of therapy.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
The predominant feature of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is poorly controlled asthma symptoms despite maximal levels of conventional therapy. Other features of vasculitis including weight loss and night sweats, and mononeuritis may be seen.

Giant-cell arteritis
Giant-cell arteritis is associated with temporal headaches and jaw claudication and is seen in older patients. It carries significant risk of ischaemic stroke and requires treatment with high-dose corticosteroids.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with pulmonary and renal haemorrhage and deteriorating renal function, but symptoms of sinusitis are usually reported, and CRP levels are usually much higher than those seen here, suggesting that anti-GBM disease is in fact the underlying diagnosis.

Lupus nephritis
Although lupus nephritis is associated with blood and proteinuria and deteriorating renal function, the short onset of symptoms including pulmonary haemorrhage in a heavy smoker is much more suggestive of anti-GBM disease. In lupus nephritis, other features such as a photosensitive rash and small-joint polyarthropathy would be expected.

stem: A 23-year-old man attends the Gastroenterology Clinic to discuss the results of his colonoscopy. He has been opening his bowels up to three times a day, with loose stools occasionally flecked with blood. He is still able to work as a trainee teacher and denies fever. The colonoscopy showed inflammation distally from the sigmoid colon, and biopsy appearance was consistent with ulcerative colitis. What is the most appropriate initial intervention for him?
explanation:
Mesalazine
Mesalazine, a 5-amino salicylic acid compound, is the initial treatment of choice for patients with mild symptoms of ulcerative colitis, as here. A number of preparations exist, including slow-release preparations which can avoid three-times-a-day dosing. For the three-times-a-day dosing, up to 2.4 g/day can be administered. It is thought to act as an anti-inflammatory agent at the level of the bowel wall. Side-effects are mainly gastrointestinal, although blood dyscrasias are also rarely seen.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is a recommended disease-modifying agent for patients requiring more than two courses of oral corticosteroids in any one year or in those patients who are steroid intolerant. If azathioprine then fails to control symptoms a tumour necrosis factor antagonist could be considered.

stem: A 57-year-old man is referred to the Neurology Clinic. He has had a chronic cough and shortness of breath over the past few months and has now developed proximal muscle weakness. He smokes 50 cigarettes per day. On examination, he has grip weakness, but this improves when he repeatedly opens and closes his hand. A chest X-ray reveals a right hilar mass. Which autoantibodies are the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies
This patient is likely to be suffering from Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome. Presynaptic voltage-gated calcium-channel antibodies are responsible for symptoms of proximal muscle weakness; unlike Guillain–Barré syndrome, it is possible for muscle strength to improve with potentiation. Amifampradine has been shown to improve muscle strength in patients with the syndrome.

Acetylcholine receptor antibodies
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies are associated with myasthenia gravis, which is associated with proximal muscle weakness but does not fit with the likely underlying bronchial carcinoma here, making Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome the more likely diagnosis.

stem: A 27-year old-woman is to be started on azathioprine for treatment of inflammatory bowel disease. Which enzyme's activity should be checked before starting azathioprine therapy?
explanation:
Thiopurine-S-methyltransferase
Thiopurine-S-methyltransferase, (TPMT) is responsible for the metabolism of azathioprine and 6- mercaptopurine, both of which are used as immunosuppressant agents. Homozygous TPMT deficiency is found in 1 in 300 individuals and can lead to significant and potentially lethal bone marrow suppression when these agents are used in a patient with the condition. High levels of the enzyme are > 150 mU/l, low levels are set at below 68 mU/l and in patients with levels below 68, an alternative therapy should be considered.

Acetylcholinesterase
Acetylcholinesterase is responsible for the breakdown of acetylcholine. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are used in the treatment of Alzheimer's dementia, donepezil is an example of the class.

Catechol-O-methyltransferase
Catecholamine-O-methyltransferase (COMT) is responsible for the metabolism of levodopa. Use of COMT inhibitors can ameliorate fluctuations in levodopa in patients treated for Parkinson's disease and reduce on–off phenomena.

stem: A 22-year-old woman is commenced on the combined oral contraceptive pill and is concerned about risk of developing cancer. Risk of which cancer is reduced by taking the oral contraceptive pill?
explanation:
Colon
Oral contraceptive pill use is associated with a 15–20% relative risk reduction in new cases of colorectal cancer. The reason this reduction in colon cancer occurs is unclear; it may be related to reduced ovulations and consequent fluctuation in female hormones or due to changes in bile-salt metabolism in response to contraceptive pill use. The risk of ovarian cancer is also significantly reduced in patients who are users of the combined oral contraceptive pill.

Breast
An increased risk of developing breast cancer between 20% and 60% is associated with oral contraceptive pill use. Risk for developing breast cancer is thought to increase with prolonged exposure.

Cervical
Risk of cervical cancer is seen to increase in patients who use the oral contraceptive pill with Chatlonger with AIduration Tutor of exposure. The reason for this is unclear; it may be that women who use the oral contraceptive pill have increased susceptibility to high-risk human papillomavirus subtypes.

stem: A 21-year-old man is referred to the Endocrine Clinic. He has an elevated fasting glucose of 8.1 mmol/l and has suffered from recurrent episodes of genital candidiasis. He has not lost any weight and does not have polydipsia. His body mass index is 23 kg/m 2. Which of the following is most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
MODY-3
According to prevalence estimates MODY-3 makes up 30–60% of cases of the disease. It is due to mutations in the HNF1-alpha gene. It is characterised by progressive onset of hyperglycaemia, with most cases of diabetes mellitus presenting by age 25. The gene mutation leads to a defect in insulin secretion. Patients often respond to sulphonylureas for some time before needing to transition to insulin therapy.

MODY-1
MODY-1 is less common, making up 5–10% of cases of MODY. It occurs due to a mutation in the HNF4-alpha gene which leads to a progressive insulin secretory defect.

MODY-2
MODY-2 accounts for 30–50% of cases of MODY. It is unlikely to be the diagnosis here because it is usually asymptomatic and diagnosed as an incidental finding when glycosuria is discovered.

stem: A 56-year-old man who was ventilated for four weeks for COVID-19 infection is recovering on the Respiratory Ward. He feels tired and is taking some time to mobilise with the help of physios. Investigation Result Normal value Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) 0.4 mU/l 0.4–4.5 mU/l Free thyroxine (T4) 6.5 pmol/l 7.9–14.4 pmol/l Free triiodothyronine (T3) 3.7 pmol/l 3.8–6.0 pmol/l What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Euthyroid sick syndrome
Euthyroid sick syndrome is seen following a period of severe illness such as prolonged COVID-19 infection. It is characterised by a slight reduction across the range of thyroid hormones including TSH, T3 and T4. A slow improvement in thyroid status usually follows recovery from the intercurrent illness, and no further intervention is required.

stem: A 56-year-old woman presents to the Hepatology Clinic with progressive lethargy and itching over the past six months. She drinks 4 units of alcohol per week. She has evidence of jaundiced sclerae and scratch marks. She has right upper quadrant pain and one finger's breadth hepatomegaly on abdominal examination. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 102 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 65 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 86 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3,9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 97 µmol/l 60–90 µmol/l Alkaline phosphatase 310 IU/l 30–130 IU/l Alanine aminotransferase 87 IU/l 0–34 IU/l Bilirubin 45 micromol/l < 21 µmol/l What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Anti-mitochondrial antibodies
A clinical scenario of slowly progressive obstructive jaundice in a middle-aged woman fits best with a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are present in 0.5% of the general population and 95% or more of patients with primary biliary cholangitis, making it the initial investigation of choice. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the intervention of choice, although a Cochrane meta-analysis failed to prove definitive benefit.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is an invasive investigation, and because of that, it carries risk of procedural morbidity and mortality. It is mainly considered where there is common bile-duct obstruction which may benefit from sphincterotomy (for example, for gallstone removal).

Liver biopsy
Liver biopsy is usually considered if antibody testing for primary biliary cholangitis, the likely diagnosis here, is not diagnostic (anti-mitochondrial antibodies are usually seen). In this case, anti-mitochondrial antibodies are the most appropriate initial investigation.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography in primary biliary cholangitis shows segmental areas of hepatic atrophy or hypertrophy, the surface of the liver is irregular, and a parenchymal lace-like fibrosis pattern may be seen.

Ultrasound abdomen
This patients prolonged history of tiredness and itching fits best with a chronic obstructive process, most likely primary biliary cholangitis. Ultrasound is considered as an investigation but it is most useful to rule out alternative causes of biliary obstruction, such as gallstone disease.

stem: A 73-year-old man is referred to the Respiratory Clinic with shortness of breath, a dry cough and gradually deteriorating exercise tolerance. He has finger clubbing and there are bilateral inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 140 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count 9.9 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l (WCC) C-reactive protein 45 mg/l < 10 mg/l (CRP) Platelets (PLT) 197 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 99 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Evidence of fibrosis with cyst formation and honeycombing; changes are more marked at the lung bases What is the best way to monitor disease progression in this patient?
options: Forced expiratory volume in one second
explanation:
Forced vital capacity
This patient has symptoms consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, for which forced vital capacity (FVC) is the most appropriate repeat investigation to monitor disease progression. An FVC above 80% at the point of diagnosis according to National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines allows the progression of nintedanib, which has been shown to slow progression of disease.

Autoantibody titre
Anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies may be found in up to 45% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. They are not used to monitor disease progression, for which FVC is the most useful investigation.

Forced expiratory volume in one second
FEV 1 is most useful as a measure of obstructive lung disease. In this case, the symptoms are consistent with restrictive lung disease, for which FVC is the most useful measure of disease progression.

Pulse oximetry
Pulse oximetry may show persistent hypoxia in advanced pulmonary fibrosis, but to monitor the effect of intervention in earlier disease, FVC is the most useful investigation.

Repeat CT scanning
Repeat CT scanning may be indicated if there is a rapid deterioration in this patient's symptoms which might indicate a cause apart from disease progression such as acute infection. For routine monitoring of disease, FVC is the most appropriate investigation.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is reviewed in the Cardiac Genetics Clinic because she is worried about her risk of sudden death. Her mother died in her sleep when she was 23-years old and her aunt died in her sleep aged 24. Her 12-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with a QT interval of 370 milliseconds (<450 milliseconds). What is the most likely mode of inheritance of her cardiac disease?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Brugada syndrome follows an autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern, and unlike other conditions such as hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and congenital long QT syndrome, which are associated with arrhythmias precipitated by exercise or high emotion, it is associated with sudden death in bed. The ECG in Brugada syndrome follows a right bundle branch block pattern, but in this case, because it is inherited in autosomal-dominant fashion, the unaffected patient described here has a normal ECG. In patients with the condition, an implantable cardioverter defibrillator is required.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal-recessive atrial dilative cardiomyopathy is well described. Many other forms of cardiac disease, including most forms of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy and Brugada syndrome, are inherited in autosomal-dominant pattern.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is prescribed sumatriptan to use for treatment of acute migraine. She does not want to take prophylactic therapy. What is the site of action of sumatriptan?
explanation:
5-HT1 receptors
Sumatriptan is a specific and selective 5-HT 1d-receptor agonist, it has not demonstrated activity on the other 5- HT-receptor subtypes. The vascular 5-HT 1d-receptor is found predominantly in cranial blood vessels and drives vasoconstriction. It is thought that by driving vasoconstriction in meningeal vessels and reducing oedema, sumatriptan reduces symptoms of headache. It should not be used in patients with symptoms of angina or unstable coronary artery disease.

5-HT2 receptors
5-HT2 receptors are distributed in the CNS, and atypical antipsychotics are drugs that act as antagonists at the 5-HT2A receptor. Examples include risperidone and olanzapine.

5-HT3 receptors
5-HT3-receptor antagonists are used in the management of emesis related to cancer chemotherapy. 5-HT3 receptors are found both in the CNS and in the peripheral nervous system. Examples include ondansetron and granisetron.

stem: An 18-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with symptoms of severe acne which she has had for three years. Which of the following is a main trigger for acne in young women?
explanation:
Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation
Follicular epidermal hyperproliferation is thought to be a key step in the development of acne. It is followed by subsequent follicle plugging and excess sebum production. Subsequently, inflammation develops which may be accentuated by colonisation with C. acnes. In men, and in women with polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), excess androgens may also contribute to the development of acne lesions.

Androgen excess
Androgen excess is a driver primarily for the development and worsening of acne in men and in women with PCOS. As most young women do not have PCOS, androgen excess is unlikely to be a main driver for acne.

Capillary hyperaemia
Capillary hyperaemia is most important as a driver for the development of rosacea rather than acne vulgaris. In this case it is follicular epidermal hyperproliferation which is thought to be the inciting event for acne.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to the Cancer Genetics Clinic. She has just been found to have the BRCA1 mutation. Her mother and aunt died of breast cancer in their 40s. What is the percentage chance of the patient developing breast cancer by age 80?
explanation:
48%
BRCA1 encodes for a tumour-suppressor gene, and mutations in BRCA1 are particularly associated with increased risk of breast and ovarian cancers in women. Penetrance of BRCA1 with respect to cases of breast cancer is however incomplete; trials estimate that the risk of breast cancer by age 80 is 48%. This may be due to co-inheritance of genes that are protective against breast cancer.

12%
The penetrance of breast cancer is much higher than 12% in association with the BRCA1 mutation. By age 80 it approaches 48%. For ovarian cancer, the risk to age 80 is 22%.

24%
24% approximates to the risk of ovarian cancer for both BRCA1 and BRCA2, which is put at around 22% by age 80. Penetrance may be higher in certain individuals dependent on environmental factors and other genes that may be co-inherited.

stem: A 57-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with episodes of nausea, diarrhoea, facial flushing, shortness of breath and palpitations some 15–30 minutes after eating a meal. He underwent a partial gastrectomy for peptic ulcer disease three months ago. What is the most appropriate initial intervention for him?
options: Frequent, small meals high in simple sugars
explanation:
Frequent, small, high-fibre, high-protein meals
This patient has symptoms of gastric dumping, for which a change in eating pattern to regular, small meals, high in protein and fibre are the initial intervention of choice. Symptoms have probably developed post-surgery because of loss of function of the pyloric sphincter. Octreotide may be of value in patients with severe symptoms.

Domperidone
Domperidone is a prokinetic agent. This patient has symptoms of dumping syndrome due to too-rapid passage of food from the stomach into the small intestine, for which domperidone will have no value as an intervention. Small, regular meals, high in protein and fibre are the intervention of choice.

stem: A 74-year-old man is reviewed on the Stroke Ward one week after suffering a right-sided anterior circulation stroke. His current performance is scored using the Barthel Index. Which of the following is a component of the Barthel Index?
explanation:
Dressing
Dressing is an activity of daily living which forms part of the Barthel Index. Three levels of score are assessed, independent (which scores 10 points), assisted which scores 5, and unable which scores 0. Other factors assessed include bladder control, bowel control, toilet use, ability to transfer, mobility on a level surface, mobility on stairs, feeding, bathing and grooming. The maximum score is 100.

Clock drawing
The clock-drawing test is a complex drawing task used to assess dementia status. It can also be used to assess executive function and visual–spatial function which are related to parietal lobe function. It is not part of the Barthel Index which measures activities of daily living.

Counting backwards
Counting backwards is a test of concentration which is assessed in the mini-mental state test. Spelling a word backwards can be used as an alternative. Concentration can be particularly affected in Alzheimer's disease.

stem: A 42-year-old woman is undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer and is prescribed granisetron as part of her antiemetic regimen. What is the mode of action of granisetron?
explanation:
5-HT3-receptor antagonist
5-HT3 receptors are present in both the central and the peripheral nervous system, and 5-HT3 antagonists such as granisetron and ondansetron (the original member of the class) block these receptors, giving them antiemetic properties. Headache, fatigue and constipation are possible adverse effects of therapy, and QT prolongation is also seen with members of the class.

5-HT1-receptor partial agonist
5-HT1-receptor partial agonists are used as antidepressants. Buspirone is an example of a 5-HT1-receptor partial agonist. It may be particularly useful in treating depression where there are prominent features of anxiety.

5-HT2-receptor antagonist
5-HT2 antagonists are not used as antiemetics. In fact, their main role is as antidepressants. Trazodone is an example of a 5-HT2A-receptor antagonist used to treat major depressive disorder. It also has antagonist effects at histamine-H1 receptors and is an antagonist of alpha-1-adrenergic receptors.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a follow-up urine sample after five days' treatment for a suspected lower UTI. She has been taking ibuprofen for menstrual cramps but is otherwise well. Investigation Result Normal value Initial urine sample No growth at 48 h Follow-up sample Leukocytes positive, red cells and protein negative C-reactive protein (CRP) 11 mg/l < 10 mg/l What is the most likely cause of her urinary leukocytosis?
explanation:
NSAIDs
Sterile pyuria is seen in conjunction with use of a number of medications including NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, corticosteroids and proton-pump inhibitors. Given this patient's urinary tract symptoms have resolved it seems like ibuprofen is the likely culprit for the urinary leukocytes seen here.

Chlamydia
Although chlamydia has to be cultured on special media, there is no indication here of a sexually transmitted infection, especially as now the patient has no symptoms. It is most likely that use of ibuprofen has led to sterile pyuria in this case.

stem: A 38-year-old man who has essential hypertension presents to the Emergency Department complaining of headache, pain down the left side of his neck and blurred vision affecting his left eye. There is a partial ptosis of the left eye and miosis of the pupil. What is the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
Magnetic resonance angiography
The symptoms reported here are highly suggestive of carotid artery dissection, for which Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is the most sensitive way to confirm the diagnosis. As here, up to 50% of patients may present with Horner syndrome on the same side as the dissection. Management is aimed at prevention of cerebral infarction and both anticoagulation and thrombolysis are possible interventions in patients with features of a stroke. Endovascular stenting is safe and effective in appropriate patients.

Carotid duplex scanning
Carotid duplex scanning is less sensitive versus MRA in identifying a carotid dissection, and an MRA has the advantage of identifying anatomy to evaluate potential surgical approaches or endovascular stenting.

stem: A 28-year-old woman is referred to the Neurology Clinic complaining of difficulty walking. She has had multiple sclerosis (MS) for the past 12 years. She is keen to continue her job as a solicitor for as long as possible. On examination, there is pyramidal weakness of the left leg with stiffness of the hamstring. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Botulinum toxin
In this case with spasticity isolated to the hamstring, and the patient holding a demanding job as a solicitor, local therapy is preferred at least initially. Botulinum toxin has been extensively used in combination with physiotherapy to treat spasticity and is the option of choice here. It may need to be repeated every 3–4 months. Baclofen is the initial systemic therapy of choice.

Baclofen
Baclofen is the usual first-line systemic therapy for treatment of muscle spasticity in MS and in patients post- stroke. In this case, however, spasticity is localised to the hamstrings, meaning local therapy with botulinum toxin is an appropriate first-line option. Overtreatment with systemic therapy can lead to low tone, and therefore, falls or arm weakness can occur.

stem: A 45-year-old man is referred to the Hypertension Clinic. He is currently taking ramipril 10 mg per day. His BP is 159/89 mmHg and heart rate is 74 bpm and regular. His BMI is 24 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 137 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 5.8 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 302 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 3.1 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Bicarbonate (HCO3) 33 mmol/l 22–28 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 95 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l What is the most likely underlying cause of his hypertension?
explanation:
Hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism
Hypertension with hypokalaemia in the presence of maximally dosed angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is highly suggestive of hyporeninaemic hyperaldosteronism related either to adrenal hyperplasia AI an or to Tutor adrenal adenoma. Ideally, renin and aldosterone should be measured off medication to confirm the diagnosis.

stem: A 74-year-old man is reviewed on the Orthopaedic Ward. He was admitted following a fall and was unconscious with a sodium level of 108 mmol/l. He was given 1.8% saline and his sodium is now 130 mmol/l some 24 hours later. He appears conscious and can move his eyes but is unable to move all four limbs. What is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Central pontine myelinolysis
The maximum rate recommended for correction of serum sodium in hyponatraemia is 6–12 mmol/l in the first 24 hours. This is to prevent central pontine myelinolysis, which can lead to permanent quadraplegia. Central pontine myelinolysis fits with the symptoms seen here where consciousness and eye movements are preserved but limb movements are lost. Patients with severe hyponatraemia should be managed with gradual correction of sodium in an environment where it can be controlled, such as a High Dependency Unit.

Basilar artery stroke
A basilar artery stroke can lead to a locked-in-syndrome picture. However, in this case, the most likely cause of quadraplegia is very rapid correction of sodium and central pontine myelinolysis, because hypertonic saline has been given and the rate of correction is at least twice that recommended.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is about to start induction chemotherapy for the treatment of acute myeloid leukaemia. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 79 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 102.1 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 76 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.3 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 122 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Which of the following medications is most useful in preventing deterioration of renal function?
explanation:
Rasburicase
Rasburicase is recombinant urate oxidase which promotes oxidation of uric acid to water and allantoin, which are both water soluble and can be excreted harmlessly in urine. It is important to consider it for pre-treatment of patients with haematological malignancy undergoing induction chemotherapy because they are at high risk of acute urate nephropathy due to massive cell lysis of leukaemic cells. An initial dose of 3 Chat mg ofwith rasburicase IV is recommended at the time of starting chemotherapy.

stem: A 74-year-old man who has severe bone pain from multiple myeloma presents to the Oncology Clinic with worsening pain. His current slow-release morphine dose is 60 mg twice day. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 97 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 8.1 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 153 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 142 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l What is the most appropriate morphine dose every 2–4 hours for breakthrough pain?
explanation:
20 mg
The recommendation to control breakthrough pain is to use one-sixth of the total daily dose of slow-release morphine, which can be given every 2–4 hours. Under-dosing may not control pain and overdosing may lead to somnolence and confusion. In patients with moderate renal impairment, use of lower doses of morphine is required or potential switching to an opiate subject to less dose accumulation such as oxycodone.

stem: A 78-year-old man, who has Parkinson's disease, is brought to his General Practitioner by his daughter, as she is concerned about his behaviour. Since a change in medication, he has begun to gamble excessively on horse racing and has exhibited other risk-taking behaviours. Which medication is most likely to be the cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Ropinirole
Ropinirole is a dopamine agonist. In Parkinson's disease the class of drugs has been shown to potentiate risk taking, including compulsive gambling, spending large amounts of money and other actions such as risky sexual behaviour. Although the class is very effective in controlling Parkinson's symptoms, patients and their relatives should be warned of this potential side-effect.

Co-careldopa
Co-careldopa is often used as an initial therapy for Parkinson's disease. Adverse effects of therapy can include dizziness, nausea and sleep disturbance. Impulsive behaviour is a hallmark adverse effect of dopamine-agonist therapy.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred to the Respiratory Clinic complaining of worsening asthma symptoms despite high-dose inhaled corticosteroids, a long-acting beta-agonist and montelukast. Most recently, she has also suffered from a common peroneal nerve palsy affecting her left lower limb. Auscultation of the chest reveals wheeze throughout both lung fields. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 118 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.3 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l Eosinophil count 3.4 × 10 9/l 0.05–0.50 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 89 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 304 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 143 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 112 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Blood 2+ Urine analysis Protein 2+ What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is associated with asthma symptoms which do not respond to conventional therapy, a rise in peripheral blood eosinophil count and other features of vasculitis such as mononeuritis and blood and proteinuria. Approximately 30–40% of patients with the disease have positive perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA). High-dose corticosteroids are the mainstay of therapy; second-line interventions include ciclosporin, azathioprine and rituximab.

Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease
Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease is associated with antibodies against the glomerular basement membrane; it leads to pulmonary and vascular haemorrhage, with a rapid deterioration in renal function. Plasma exchange is the intervention of choice.

Giant-cell arteritis
Giant-cell arteritis is associated with temporal headaches and jaw claudication and occurs in older patients. There is normally a significant rise in erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and a rapid response to corticosteroids.

Microscopic polyangiitis
Microscopic polyangiitis is associated with signs of renal and gastrointestinal haemorrhage and other features of vasculitis, including mononeuritis. The features of worsening asthma seen here, however, are much more consistent with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is associated with renal vasculitis, as seems likely with the elevated creatinine and blood and proteinuria seen here. It is also, however, usually associated with small-joint polyarthritis and a rash on sun-exposed areas, and not with worsening symptoms of asthma as we've seen here.

stem: A 27-year-old woman, who is 29 weeks' pregnant, presents to the Emergency Department with pain in her left calf and left-sided pleuritic chest pain. Her left calf is mildly tender and is 4 cm greater in diameter than the right calf. Her BP is 122/72 mmHg and heart rate is 95 bpm at rest. Her chest is clear on auscultation. What is the most useful next investigation?
options: Duplex ultrasound of the left leg
explanation:
Duplex ultrasound of the left leg
Compression duplex ultrasound of the left leg is the most appropriate next investigation when there are symptoms of a DVT as here. Assuming DVT is confirmed, no further investigations are necessary, pulmonary embolism in addition to DVT is presumed and anticoagulation commenced.

Chest X-ray
CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) and ventilation perfusion scanning can both be used to diagnose pulmonary embolism in pregnancy. In this situation, however, with features of DVT, a duplex ultrasound of the left leg is the most appropriate next step.

CT pulmonary angiogram
Given there are no chest signs on auscultation, and performing a chest X-ray still involves exposure to radiation, it is not indicated here. Given there are signs of a DVT, a compression duplex ultrasound of the left leg is most appropriate.

stem: A 73-year-old man is referred to the Respiratory Clinic with progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough. He has night sweats and has lost 6 kg in weight over the past few months. He smokes ten cigarettes per day. His BP is 132/82 mmHg, heart rate is 78 bpm and regular. He has finger clubbing and bilateral inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. His BMI is 22kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 129 g/l 135–175 g/l White cell count (WCC) 9.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 54 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 189 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 89 µmol/l 60–120 µmol/l Anti-nuclear antibody Positive Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV 1) 55% of predicted Forced vital capacity (FVC) 65% of predicted What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Systemic lupus erythematosus related lung disease
explanation:
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis occurs in the absence of other precipitants such as underlying autoimmune disease or exposure to asbestos. It fits with the clinical picture seen here with a marked reduction in FEV 1 and FVC, signs of pulmonary fibrosis on auscultation of the chest and finger clubbing. A high-resolution CT scan to confirm the presence of fibrosis is the next most appropriate step in investigation.

Asbestosis
Asbestosis can present with a restrictive lung picture on lung function testing, although there is usually a clear trigger with respect to asbestos exposure which is not identified here.

Asthma
Asthma is associated with an obstructive picture on lung function testing, rather than the restrictive picture seen here. The restrictive picture coupled with crackles on auscultation and finger clubbing is more consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is associated with smoking and has an obstructive picture on lung function testing. It does not fit with the finger clubbing and restrictive picture on spirometry which is consistent with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Systemic lupus erythematosus related lung disease
Although systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can lead to pulmonary fibrosis, there are no other features of SLE reported here such as joint pains or a photosensitive rash. Anti-nuclear antibodies are commonly found in the general population without underlying autoimmune disease.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is reviewed in the Rheumatology Clinic. She has a small-joint polyarthritis which has responded initially to a reducing dose of oral prednisolone. She is rheumatoid factor positive. She is not interested in having children now. What is the most appropriate initial maintenance therapy for this patient?
explanation:
Methotrexate
Weekly methotrexate is the intervention of choice for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis. The usual starting dose is 7.5 mg weekly. This can be increased to a dose of around 20 mg weekly. It is given in conjunction with folic acid. Methotrexate is associated with a risk of hepatic fibrosis, so regular monitoring of liver function is essential.

Azathioprine
Azathioprine is an alternative disease-modifying agent to methotrexate. It is thought to be less effective. It can be considered in females intending to get pregnant, as it is the safest immune-modifying agent in pregnancy.

Infliximab
Infliximab is a tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha antagonist. TNF-alpha antagonists are the add-in choice where methotrexate alone fails to control symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis. Use of infliximab can risk reactivation of tuberculosis and worsening of underlying viral hepatitis.

stem: The performance of a new biomarker for medullary thyroid cancer is tested in a screening study. Results are shown below: Thyroid cancer confirmed Thyroid cancer negative Marker positive 130 5 Marker negative 25 100 What is the positive predictive value for this test?
explanation:
96%
96% is the positive predictive value, a measure of precision, which calculates the percentage of positive-test patients that have the disease. In this case, 130 / (130 + 5) = 0.96 or 96%.

5%
This is 1 minus the specificity, which is known as the likelihood ratio. It is defined as the ratio of the true-positive rate divided by the false-positive rate.

stem: A 45-year-old woman, who smokes ten cigarettes per day, is referred to the Respiratory Clinic. She has frequent episodes of winter bronchitis and has failed to gain significant benefit from a salbutamol inhaler given by her General Practitioner. Her BP is 123/82 mmHg and heart rate is 75 bpm and regular. There is scattered wheeze on auscultation of the chest. Her BMI is 23 kg/m 2. Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 130 g/l 120–160 g/l White cell count (WCC) 7.2 × 10 9/l 4.0–11.0 × 10 9/l C-reactive protein (CRP) 8 mg/l < 10 mg/l Platelets (PLT) 235 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 142 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.5 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Creatinine (Cr) 90 µmol/l 50–90 µmol/l Forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV 1) 55% of predicted > 80% of predicted FEV 1/forced vital capacity (FVC) 58% > 70% What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
The patient's smoking history and age make COPD the most likely cause of her symptoms. The significantly reduced FEV1 (55% of predicted) and FEV1/FVC ratio (58%) confirm an obstructive pattern on spirometry testing. The lack of significant response to salbutamol further supports the diagnosis. Combination therapy with a long-acting beta-agonist and long-acting muscarinic antagonist, along with strong advice to stop smoking, would be the most appropriate next step.

Asthma
Given this patient's smoking history, COPD is a more likely diagnosis than asthma. Earlier onset of symptoms is usually seen in asthma, and symptoms are variable, especially in response to seasonal allergy triggers.

Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is associated with coughing up large volumes of purulent sputum. Finger clubbing is also seen and coarse crackles are usually present at the lung basis on auscultation.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is associated with inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest and a restrictive picture on lung function testing which does not fit with the clinical picture seen here.

Obliterative bronchiolitis
Obliterative bronchiolitis does result in an obstructive picture on pulmonary function testing which responds poorly to bronchodilator therapy. It is, however, associated with autoimmune disease, including rheumatoid arthritis, not present here.

stem: A 79-year-old man is brought to his General Practitioner by his son. He has been suffering from intermittent confusion and fluctuating difficulty in carrying out routine daily tasks. He has a 2-year history of recurrent falls, depressed mood and intermittent visual hallucinations. On examination, he has a shuffling gait with reduced arm swing bilaterally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dementia with Lewy bodies
Dementia with Lewy bodies would be most in keeping with the clinical presentation here. The key features which make this most likely are the marked fluctuations in cognition and visual hallucinations, as well as evidence of extrapyramidal signs on examination. Movement disorders in dementia with Lewy bodies share significant overlap with those seen in Parkinson’s disease. However, crucially, in dementia with Lewy bodies, cognitive symptoms occur early followed by mild pyramidal features (and/or myoclonus) whereas in Parkinson’s disease dementia, extrapyramidal motor symptoms/signs precede the dementia by years.

Alzheimer’s dementia
While Alzheimer’s dementia is the most common dementia, this patient’s fluctuating cognition, recurrent falls and visual hallucinations make dementia with Lewy bodies more likely. Alzheimer’s dementia is classically associated with amnesia, aphasia, apraxia and agnosia.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with a 2-day history of progressive, severe, retro- orbital headache, myalgia, nausea and vomiting. She had returned from Indonesia three days previously. On examination, her temperature is 39.5 °C, and BP is 125/70 mmHg lying and 105/65 mmHg standing. She is dehydrated and has a petechial rash over her trunk and limbs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal value Haemoglobin (Hb) 149 g/l 115–155 g/l White cell count (WCC) 4.1 × 10 9/l 4–11 × 10 9/l Platelets (PLT) 95 × 10 9/l 150–400 × 10 9/l Sodium (Na +) 141 mmol/l 135–145 mmol/l Potassium (K +) 4.9 mmol/l 3.5–5.0 mmol/l Urea 15.0 mmol/l 2.5–6.5 mmol/l Creatinine 187 µmol/l 50–120 µmol/l Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 280 IU/l 5–30 IU/l Blood film (thick and thin) Negative for malarial parasites What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
Paracetamol and rehydration
This patient has dengue fever: she has travelled to an at-risk area and has developed a fever with thrombocytopenia and a petechial rash, in conjunction with the classical retro-orbital headache and flu-like symptoms. No specific treatment is required: supportive therapy with paracetamol and rehydration is adequate. Occasionally, in severe cases, clotting factors may be required. Diagnosis is via serology; however, due to the specialist nature of these serological tests, results will often not be available for 1–2 weeks, and patients must be treated according to clinical suspicion.

Aciclovir
Aciclovir is an appropriate treatment for suspected encephalitis, which may present with severe headache. However, this patient’s symptoms and signs are more suggestive of dengue fever: she has travelled to an endemic area, and retro-orbital headache, flu-like illness, fever, and thrombocytopenia with deranged liver function tests are typical. Dengue fever is caused by a mosquito-borne virus. Treatment is supportive; it is a haemorrhagic fever and in severe cases, clotting factors may be required; otherwise, paracetamol and rehydration are the only treatments required.

Benzylpenicillin
Intramuscular benzylpenicillin is an appropriate primary care treatment for suspected meningococcal meningitis; as this patient has a rash, fever and severe headache, this is an understandable differential diagnosis. However, given her travel history, the retro-orbital nature of the headache and her thrombocytopenia and deranged liver function tests, dengue fever is the likely diagnosis here. This is a virus carried by mosquitoes, and does not require treatment with antibiotics. In fact, the most appropriate treatment is supportive, with paracetamol and fluids. It is a haemorrhagic fever and, in severe cases, patients may require clotting factor replacement.

Ceftriaxone
Ceftriaxone would be an appropriate treatment for meningococcal meningitis; however, this patient has symptoms and signs that suggest dengue fever, rather than meningitis. A severe, retro-orbital headache is a classic symptom of dengue fever, and she has travelled from an area where dengue is endemic. Her thrombocytopenia, petechial rash and deranged liver function tests are also suggestive of dengue fever. The most appropriate treatment for this viral haemorrhagic fever is supportive, with paracetamol and fluids. Rarely, in severe cases, patients may require clotting factors.

Ibuprofen
This patient has dengue fever: she has returned from an at-risk area, has a petechial rash, thrombocytopenia, deranged liver function tests and a severe retro-orbital headache with flu-like symptoms. stem: A 50-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department having woken with visual blurring and an inability to appreciate colours in the left eye, as well as the right eye. She has a history of hypertension, for which she takes amlodipine, and type II diabetes, for which she takes metformin. Her BP is 135/80 mmHg and she has a regular pulse of 72 bpm. Her BMI is 27 kg/m 2. Fundoscopy reveals a swollen left optic disc, and visual-field testing reveals a loss of vision inferiorly in the left eye. What is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation:
Optic nerve
The altitudinal field defect, apparent loss of visual acuity and swollen disc points towards ischaemic optic neuropathy, probably non-artertic, given the age and lack of presenting features of giant-cell arteritis (pointing towards arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy).

Occipital lobe
Lesions in the occipital lobe would not be consistent with the above presentation, but rather cause cortical blindness or, in the context of occipital lobe seizures, flashing lights or colours.

stem: A 47-year-old woman is referred to the Neurology Clinic suffering from right-sided headaches that occur around her right eye. They last from 15 minutes to two hours and can occur up to 3–4 times per day, beginning at around the same time each evening. She says the headaches cause sharp, severe pain, as well as tearing and redness of the right eye. Neurological examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cluster headache
Cluster headache fits with this patient’s symptoms of unilateral headache affecting the area around the eye, accompanied by autonomic symptoms such as tearing and conjunctival injection. The duration of the headaches, occurring over a short, predictable period of the day, also fits with the diagnosis. High-flow oxygen is useful for acute treatment of the headaches. Over the longer-term, verapamil is effective as prophylaxis – it can be used at a total daily dose of up to 480 mg.

Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is associated with headaches which are worse on lying flat and on straining, and may be associated with visual obscurations and tinnitus. It is most commonly seen in obese young women.

stem: An 82-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with increasing oedema and ascites. He is hypertensive, for which he takes amlodipine. He has shortness of breath on exercise and drinks two cans of stout per day. An ECG is normal and chest X-ray reveals normal heart size and no signs of cardiac failure. Serum albumin is 23 g/dl; urinary albumin excretion is 7 g/24 hours, with no haematuria. He has mild anaemia, with a normal mean corpuscular volume (MCV). Total cholesterol is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Nephrotic syndrome
Low albumin, abnormal cholesterol and increased urinary albumin excretion all point towards nephrotic syndrome. In the older age group, membranous nephropathy is the most common cause. Although it may be idiopathic, it can occur in association with Hodgkin’s lymphoma, carcinoma, systemic lupus erythematosus or gold therapy. Minimal-change nephropathy occurs more commonly in children.

Cardiac failure
This patient's symptoms and examination findings may be caused by heart failure, but the hypoalbuminemia and elevated protein : creatinine ratio favour nephrotic syndrome as the cause of these findings.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with sudden-onset right-sided pleuritic chest pain. He smokes five cigarettes per day and has no significant past medical illnesses. On examination his BP is 122/72 mmHg, his pulse is 88 bpm, and he is complaining of pleuritic chest pain at rest. There is decreased air entry on the right-hand side on auscultation. Chest X-ray reveals a right-sided pneumothorax with a 3 cm rim of air. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Admit for four hours for analgesia and observation
explanation:
Aspiration with a 16–18 G cannula
In this situation with a symptomatic primary pneumothorax, even a rim of air > 2 cm can be aspirated in the first instance; as such, a cannula is the most appropriate intervention. If this fails to reduce the area of air to below 2 cm or symptoms do not resolve, then a chest drain is indicated.

8–14 Fr gauge chest drain
This would have been the definitive intervention for a patient with a secondary pneumothorax of this size.

Admit for four hours for analgesia and observation
Admission for high-flow oxygen is indicated for small (1–2 cm) secondary pneumothoraces which are aspirated successfully.

stem: A 25-year-old woman receives a renal transplant for end-stage kidney disease due to type I diabetes. Three weeks later she is reviewed urgently because of deteriorating renal function. She is taking a ciclosporin-based transplant regimen and levels of cyclosporin are in the normal range. Which immune cell type is the most likely cause of her deteriorating renal function?
explanation:
Cytotoxic T cells
Early rejection, in this case occurring only three weeks after transplantation, is most likely due to cytotoxic T cells which are pre-formed against donor antigens. Unfortunately, graft loss is as high as 50%, although pulsed corticosteroids coupled with anti-T-cell antibodies may achieve salvage of the donor organ.

B cells
B cells play a role in late transplant rejection, as they differentiate to produce antibodies against the donor organ. This may be precipitated by ischaemic injury to the donor kidney driving increased release of alloantigens and local inflammation. Early rejection is driven by cytotoxic T cells.

Eosinophils
Eosinophils are not a key driver for acute rejection in renal transplant. Some studies suggest, particularly in lung tissue, that they may even play a role in suppression of cytotoxic T-cell activity.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is prescribed hydroxycarbamide for a haematological malignancy. What is the mode of action of hydroxycarbamide?
explanation:
Ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor
The exact mode of action of hydroxycarbamide is not well described, although a substantial proportion of its effect is thought to come from ribonucleotide reductase inhibition. This blocks production of deoxyribonucleotides, which are the building blocks of DNA. Given the turnover of cells in bone marrow, bone marrow suppression is the major dose-limiting toxicity of hydroxycarbamide therapy. Pancreatitis and diarrhoea are also frequently described as adverse effects of therapy.

Calcineurin inhibitor
Calcineurin inhibitors bind to immunophilins, leading to reduced interleukin 2 production and reduced T-cell proliferation. Ciclosporin is an example of a calcineurin inhibitor.

DNA polymerase inhibitor
Direct and indirect DNA polymerase inhibitors are used in the treatment of cancers, and some are used in wound dressings. Topical proflavine, a direct DNA polymerase inhibitor, is used as an antiseptic in dressings. DNA damage agents such as cyclophosphamide act as indirect DNA polymerase inhibitors.
